hook: A kicked ball does two things at once: it travels across the field and it rises and falls. Trigonometry splits its velocity into those two parts, the horizontal and the vertical, so each can be handled with the one-line motion you already know.

prereq.q: Solve y = A sin θ for A.
prereq.why: Divide both sides by sin θ.

figure.caption: A velocity is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are its horizontal and vertical components.

chain.cause: A vector points at an angle to the axes
chain.effect: it forms the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs lie along the axes

chain.cause: You know the magnitude and the angle
chain.effect: the leg adjacent to the angle is A cos θ and the leg opposite it is A sin θ
the magnitude is the square root of (x-component² + y-component²), and tan θ = y-component ÷ x-component

chain.cause: You add vectors that are not along one line
chain.effect: you add their x-components and their y-components separately

ideas: SOH CAH TOA: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite/adjacent.
Components: the side adjacent to the given angle is A cos θ; the side opposite it is A sin θ. Check which axis the angle is measured from.
Back to the vector: magnitude = √(Aₓ² + A<sub>y</sub>²); angle = tan⁻¹(A<sub>y</sub>/Aₓ).
Set your calculator to degree mode. The sheet lists 37° and 53° (the 3-4-5 triangle): sin 37° ≈ 0.60, cos 37° ≈ 0.80.
Add vectors tip to tail, or by adding x-components and y-components separately.

misconception.wrong: The x-component always uses cosine and the y-component always uses sine.
misconception.right: Cosine goes with the side adjacent to the angle you are given. If the angle is measured from the vertical (or from the ramp), the horizontal component uses sine.

summary: A vector at an angle is the hypotenuse of a right triangle. The component adjacent to the given angle is A cos θ and the opposite one is A sin θ; the magnitude is the square root of the sum of the squared components. Add vectors by components, with the calculator in degree mode.
